headline.funnel_interpretation: The significant funnel plot asymmetry (egger's p=0.0076) indicates substantial publication bias in this meta-analysis on Vitamin D and bladder cancer. This specific pattern suggests that smaller studies with smaller or null effects may be underrepresented, compromising the reliability of the pooled estimate and potentially leading to an overestimation of the true association.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 10 studies yielded an effect size of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.35–1.61), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin D and bladder cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 98.13%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

sample_size.excerpt: A prospective population-based cohort of 9791 individuals from the Copenhagen City Heart Study who were free of cancer at baseline was followed from 1981-1983 until December 2008 with 100% complete follow-up. During up to 28 years of follow-up, 1081 participants developed a tobacco-related cancer and 1506 developed other cancers.

effect_size.excerpt: Also, multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for a 50% reduction in 25(OH)D were 1.20 (1.13-1.28) for any tobacco-related cancer, 1.19 (95% CI, 1.09-1.31) for lung cancer, 1.44 (1.19-1.73) for head and neck cancer, 1.28 (1.06-1.54) for bladder cancer, 1.34 (1.04-1.73) for kidney cancer, and 0.95 (0.89-1.01) for other cancers. Lower plasma 25(OH)D was associated with higher risk of tobacco-related cancers, but not with risk of other cancers.
